notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Rogers (1962): the five perceived attributes of an innovation that predict its rate of adoption.
notes.back:
Relative advantage, compatibility (with existing values, practices, needs), complexity (negative), trialability, observability.
Relative advantage and compatibility explain most of the variance; observability matters far more than engineers assume.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Rogers's five adopter categories and their approximate proportions of the population.
notes.back:
Innovators 2.5% · Early adopters 13.5% · Early majority 34% · Late majority 34% · Laggards 16%.
Defined as standard deviations from the mean adoption time on a normal curve — a modelling choice, not an empirical law.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Geoffrey Moore's 'chasm': where it sits and why it exists.
notes.back:
Between early adopters (visionaries who buy a change agent and tolerate incompleteness) and the early majority (pragmatists who buy a proven, whole product with references from peers like themselves).
Early adopters are not references for pragmatists, so momentum stalls. Cross by dominating one narrow niche with a complete solution.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Ryan & Gross (1943), hybrid seed corn in Iowa: what drove adoption, and what was the lag?
notes.back:
Farmers heard about hybrid corn from salesmen but decided based on neighbours' visible results; interpersonal networks, not information availability, governed adoption. Average lag from first awareness to full adoption was several years despite ~20% yield gain.
Founding study of diffusion research.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Griliches (1957), hybrid corn across US states: what explained differences in adoption speed?
notes.back: Profitability. Logistic S-curves in every state, but the timing of origin and the slope tracked the expected economic gain per acre, not farmer education or information access. Adoption is an economic decision before it is an informational one.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Paul David, 'The Dynamo and the Computer' (1990): why did electrification take ~40 years to show up in factory productivity?
notes.back: Central power stations existed from 1882, but electric motors passed 50% of factory drive only ~1920. Gains required abandoning the steam-era line-shaft layout for unit drive (a motor per machine), which meant redesigning buildings, workflows, and management. Complementary reorganisation, not the core technology, was the bottleneck.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The Solow paradox (1987).
notes.back: "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics." Measured US productivity growth stayed weak through the 1970s–80s despite heavy IT investment; it accelerated only in the mid-1990s. Canonical case of lag between adoption and payoff.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The productivity J-curve (Brynjolfsson, Rock, Syverson).
notes.back: General-purpose technologies require large intangible complementary investments (process redesign, skills, data) that are unmeasured as output while being made. Measured productivity first dips, then rises above trend once the intangibles pay off. Predicts an initial 'nothing is working' phase for any GPT.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Path dependence and lock-in: the QWERTY argument and its main critique.
notes.back:
David (1985): small early events plus increasing returns (network effects, learning, complementary assets) can lock in an inferior standard — QWERTY over Dvorak. Arthur formalised increasing-returns dynamics.
Critique (Liebowitz & Margolis 1990): Dvorak's superiority was poorly evidenced; lock-in to clearly inferior standards is rare because someone can profit by switching the market.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The War of Currents (1880s–90s): what actually decided AC over DC?
notes.back: A technical parameter with economic consequences: the transformer let AC be transmitted at high voltage over long distances, while DC stations served ~1–2 km. Niagara (1895–96) went to Westinghouse. Edison's safety propaganda (electrocuting animals, the electric chair) did not change the outcome. Pattern: cost structure beats narrative.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The 'sailing ship effect'.
notes.back: Incumbent technologies often improve fastest after a challenger appears: sail (clippers, iron hulls, better rigging) advanced most 1850–1890 under pressure from steam. Incumbent response can delay a transition for decades without preventing it.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Christensen's disruptive innovation: the mechanism, and the main caveat.
notes.back:
Entrants start with a product that is worse on mainstream metrics but cheaper/simpler, serving overlooked low-end or new-market customers; incumbents rationally ignore it because their best customers do not want it. The entrant then improves until it captures the mainstream.
Caveat: predictive record is weak (Lepore 2014; King & Baatartogtokh 2015); many 'disruptors' fail and many incumbents adapt.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Teece (1986): who profits from an innovation, and the EMI CT scanner example.
notes.back: Under weak appropriability, profit goes to whoever controls the complementary assets (manufacturing, distribution, service, brand). EMI invented the CT scanner (1972) but lacked US sales/service infrastructure; GE dominated the market by ~1980 and EMI exited.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Xerox PARC and the Alto: what did Xerox commercialise and what did it not, and why?
notes.back: PARC produced the GUI, mouse, Ethernet, and laser printer (~1973). Xerox commercialised the laser printer (fit the copier business; enormously profitable) but not the Alto/Star, which Apple and Microsoft later exploited. Lesson: adoption inside a firm follows fit with existing business model and sales channel, not technical merit.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Concorde (1976–2003): why a technically superior product failed commercially.
notes.back: Development cost ~£1.1bn against a £70m estimate; 1973 oil shock; sonic-boom bans over land restricted it to a few transatlantic routes; only 14 entered service. Governments kept funding because of prior spend — hence the Concorde fallacy (sunk-cost) as a named pattern.
notes.source: Standard economic history; Dawkins & Carlisle 1976 coined 'Concorde fallacy'

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Iridium (1998): what changed between design and launch?
notes.back: $5bn, 66 satellites, ~11-year development. Meanwhile terrestrial cellular coverage expanded and shrank the addressable market; the handset was bulky, expensive, and did not work indoors. Bankrupt after nine months; assets later sold for ~$25m. Pattern: frozen market assumptions across a long build cycle.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Segway (2001): failure pattern.
notes.back: Extreme pre-launch hype ('bigger than the PC'), $5,000 price, regulatory ambiguity (sidewalk or road?), and no job it did clearly better than walking, cycling, or driving. Forecast 10,000/week; sold ~140,000 in two decades. Pattern: a solution before a problem plus unresolved legal category.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Google Glass (2013): what killed consumer adoption?
notes.back: Not the technology — social acceptability. Face-mounted cameras violated privacy norms in bars, restaurants, and conversation ('glasshole'); venues banned it. Withdrawn from consumers 2015, retargeted to enterprise. Pattern: norms and observability of use, not specs.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Betamax vs VHS: the factors usually cited for VHS winning despite Betamax's picture quality.
notes.back: VHS offered 2-hour recording (a full film) versus Beta's 1 hour at launch; JVC licensed liberally while Sony kept control; more manufacturers meant lower prices; rental stores and studios then tipped to VHS via content-availability network effects. Pattern: openness plus the use case that matters to the buyer.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Minitel (France, 1982–2012): success pattern and failure pattern in one case.
notes.back: Success: state-issued free terminals plus kiosk billing (telco collects, service gets a cut) — 25 million users, thousands of services. Failure: the installed base and business model became lock-in that delayed French internet adoption by years. State-driven success can create its own path-dependence trap.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Containerisation (McLean, 1956): why did it take ~15 years to take off?
notes.back: The box was trivial; adoption required ISO standardisation (1968–70), rebuilt ports with cranes, new ships, rail integration, and union settlements (ILA/ILWU) over lost jobs. Once in place, freight costs collapsed and trade patterns reorganised. Pattern: standards + complementary infrastructure + labour politics.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Semmelweis (1847): the evidence, the rejection, and the named pattern.
notes.back: Chlorine hand-washing cut maternal mortality in his ward from ~18% to ~2%. Rejected: no mechanism (pre germ theory), it implied physicians were killers, he was a junior outsider and communicated badly. Adopted only after Pasteur and Lister. The Semmelweis reflex: reflexive rejection of evidence that contradicts established norms.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Scurvy: from Lind's trial (1747) to Navy adoption (1795), and how the knowledge was later lost.
notes.back: Lind ran a controlled comparison showing citrus cured scurvy; Royal Navy adopted lemon juice only in 1795 (~48 years). In the 19th century the Navy switched to West Indian lime (far less vitamin C) and copper-vessel processing; scurvy returned on polar expeditions. Pattern: without a mechanism, a working practice can drift into a non-working one unnoticed.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Anaesthesia (1846) spread worldwide within a year; antisepsis (Lister, 1867) took ~20 years. Why the difference?
notes.back: Anaesthesia: benefit immediate, visible, and accrued to the adopter (the surgeon) — patient stops screaming. Antisepsis: invisible mechanism, benefit delayed (infection appears days later), required accepting germ theory, and imposed tedious protocol on the adopter. Observability and adopter incentives dominate.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Continental drift (Wegener, 1912): why rejected, and what changed in the 1960s?
notes.back: Wegener had matching coastlines, fossils, and strata but no plausible mechanism for continents ploughing through oceanic crust. Acceptance came with paleomagnetic reversals, seafloor spreading (Hess), and Vine–Matthews (1963) — a mechanism plus a decisive new instrument-generated dataset.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Planck's principle and the empirical test of it.
notes.back: "Science advances one funeral at a time." Azoulay, Fons-Rosen & Graff Zivin (2019): after the premature death of a star scientist, publications by their collaborators fall while outsiders' entry and citations in the subfield rise. Incumbency effects are real and measurable.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The Boulton & Watt patent (1775–1800) as a case of intellectual property throttling adoption.
notes.back: Boldrin & Levine: steam-engine efficiency ('duty') stagnated while Watt's broad patent was in force and improved rapidly after it expired (Cornish engines, high pressure). Contested by other historians, but a standing example that appropriability regimes can slow diffusion.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Harrison's chronometer solved longitude in 1761. Why did the Navy standardise on it only decades later?
notes.back: Cost and manufacturability. A Harrison-style watch was a bespoke object; the rival lunar-distance method needed only tables. Arnold and Earnshaw's simplified designs (1780s–1800s) brought the price down; chronometers became routine issue in the 1820s–30s. Proof of concept is not the adoption bottleneck; unit cost is.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Jevons paradox (1865) and its modern name.
notes.back: Improving the efficiency of a resource lowers its effective price and can increase total consumption (Jevons on coal and steam engines). Modern: the rebound effect; when rebound exceeds 100% it is 'backfire'. Efficiency alone is not a conservation strategy.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Amara's law.
notes.back: We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run. Consistent with hype-then-lag dynamics (Solow paradox, J-curve).
notes.source: Roy Amara, Institute for the Future

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The Gartner hype cycle: stages, and its epistemic status.
notes.back:
Innovation trigger → Peak of inflated expectations → Trough of disillusionment → Slope of enlightenment → Plateau of productivity.
It is a heuristic, not an empirical regularity: many technologies die in the trough or never peak; Gartner has not published validation data. Useful as a vocabulary for expectation dynamics.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Carlota Perez: the phases of a technological revolution.
notes.back: Installation (irruption, then frenzy driven by financial capital) → turning point (bubble bursts, institutional recomposition) → deployment (synergy, maturity, driven by production capital). Five surges since 1771 (canals/water, rail/steam, steel/electricity, oil/mass production, ICT), ~50 years each.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Why bubbles can be functional for adoption: railway mania (1840s) and the dot-com fibre glut.
notes.back: Speculative overinvestment builds infrastructure that survives the crash and is then available cheaply to the next wave: UK rail mileage tripled; 1990s dark fibre later carried the 2000s web at near-zero marginal cost. Investors lose; the technology wins.
notes.source: Perez; Janeway, Doing Capitalism in the Innovation Economy

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Wright's law, with the solar and nuclear contrast.
notes.back: Unit cost falls by a fixed percentage for each doubling of cumulative production (Wright 1936, aircraft). Solar photovoltaics: ~20% per doubling (Swanson's law). Nuclear in the US and France showed negative learning — costs rose with experience (Grubler 2010) — driven by site-specific builds and regulatory ratchets. Learning rates are properties of the production system, not the physics.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Moore's law as a self-fulfilling prophecy.
notes.back: Doubling of transistor density was not a physical law but a coordination device: the industry roadmap (ITRS) told suppliers, fabs, and customers what to target and when, aligning investment. An expectation that coordinates investment can create the regularity it predicts.
notes.source: Mody, The Long Arm of Moore's Law

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: The Collingridge dilemma (1980).
notes.back: Early in a technology's life its impacts are unpredictable but it is easy to change; once impacts are clear it is entrenched and hard to change. Governance must act under uncertainty or not at all — the core problem of anticipatory regulation.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Thalidomide and the Kefauver–Harris amendments (1962).
notes.back: Thalidomide caused ~10,000 birth defects (1957–61) in Europe; FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey had withheld US approval. Congress responded by requiring proof of efficacy as well as safety before marketing. Pattern: a vivid failure produces a regulatory ratchet that then shapes all subsequent adoption in the sector.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Hindenburg (1937): what it illustrates about salience versus statistics.
notes.back: One filmed, narrated disaster (36 deaths) ended passenger airship travel, though the technology was already losing to aircraft. A single legible catastrophe can end a technology regardless of its actuarial safety record. Compare nuclear after Three Mile Island and Fukushima.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Richard Gabriel's 'Worse is Better' (1989).
notes.back: Systems that are simple to implement, even if incomplete or inconsistent for users (Unix, C), spread faster than systems that are 'the right thing' (Lisp, ITS) because they are easy to port, understand, and improve incrementally. Implementation simplicity is an adoption feature.
notes.source: Gabriel, 'Lisp: Good News, Bad News, How to Win Big'

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::1 History of Technology and Science
notes.front: Standardisation as an adoption enabler: what standards actually do for diffusion.
notes.back: Reduce buyer risk (no orphaned investment), enable complementary-asset markets (parts, training, tooling), and create network effects across suppliers. Cases: ISO containers, GSM (mobile telephony in Europe vs fragmented US standards), TCP/IP over OSI. Standards wars are usually decided by installed base and openness, not technical merit.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Hume's problem of induction.
notes.back: No number of observed instances logically entails the next one; justifying induction by its past success is circular. Hume: we rely on induction by custom, not reason. Every response since (Popper, Bayesianism, reliabilism) is a way of living with this.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Popper's falsificationism: demarcation criterion and method.
notes.back: A theory is scientific iff it is falsifiable — it forbids some possible observations. Science proceeds by conjecture and refutation; confirmation is cheap, surviving severe tests is what matters. Marxism and psychoanalysis fail because they can absorb any outcome.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: The Duhem–Quine thesis and why it complicates falsification.
notes.back: Hypotheses are never tested alone but with auxiliary assumptions (instruments, background theory, ceteris paribus). A failed prediction refutes the conjunction; logic does not say which part to reject. Example: Uranus's anomalous orbit — Newton kept, Neptune posited. Falsification always involves judgement.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Kuhn: paradigm, normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution.
notes.back: Normal science solves puzzles within a paradigm (exemplars, methods, standards). Anomalies accumulate → crisis → a new paradigm wins, partly on non-rational grounds (persuasion, generational turnover). Successive paradigms are incommensurable: they disagree about what counts as a problem and as evidence.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Lakatos: research programmes, and the progressive/degenerating distinction.
notes.back: A programme has a hard core (immune by decision) and a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorb refutations. It is progressive if adjustments predict novel facts that are then confirmed; degenerating if they only accommodate known anomalies. Rationality is comparative and retrospective.
notes.source: Lakatos, 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes' (1970)

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Feyerabend's 'anything goes'.
notes.back: Every methodological rule has been violated in a successful scientific advance (Galileo used rhetoric and ad hoc moves). No fixed method; methodological pluralism is what actually works. Not 'nothing matters' but 'no rule is exceptionless'.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Bayes' theorem in odds form, and what it says evidence is.
notes.back:
Posterior odds = Prior odds × Likelihood ratio, where LR = P(E | H) / P(E | ¬H).
Evidence is anything that is more probable under one hypothesis than another. Strength of evidence is the likelihood ratio, independent of your prior.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Cromwell's rule.
notes.back: Never assign prior probability exactly 0 or 1 to an empirical proposition — no evidence could then move you. "I beseech you, in the bowels of Christ, think it possible that you may be mistaken." The formal core of holding beliefs provisionally.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Underdetermination of theory by data.
notes.back: For any body of evidence, multiple incompatible theories can fit it. Weak form (trivial): always some rival exists. Strong form (contested): empirically equivalent rivals with no evidence able to distinguish them. Theory choice therefore invokes extra-empirical virtues: simplicity, unification, fruitfulness.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Inference to the best explanation (abduction): the schema and the standard objection.
notes.back: From evidence E, infer the hypothesis H that would, if true, best explain E (loveliness: scope, mechanism, simplicity). Peirce called it abduction. Objection (van Fraassen): 'best of a bad lot' — the true explanation may not be among those considered.
notes.source: Peirce; Harman 1965; Lipton, Inference to the Best Explanation

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Hempel's raven paradox.
notes.back: 'All ravens are black' is logically equivalent to 'all non-black things are non-ravens', so a white shoe confirms it. Bayesian resolution: the white shoe does confirm, but negligibly, because non-black things vastly outnumber ravens. Confirmation comes in degrees.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Goodman's new riddle of induction ('grue').
notes.back: Define grue = green if examined before time t, blue otherwise. All emeralds observed are both green and grue; induction projects both, which conflict after t. Which predicates are projectible is not settled by logic — Goodman: by entrenchment in past practice. Induction depends on choice of categories.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Gettier problems.
notes.back: Justified true belief is insufficient for knowledge: you can be justified and right by luck (stopped clock showing the right time). Sparked the search for a fourth condition (no false lemmas, safety, sensitivity) and the reliabilist turn.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Foundationalism vs coherentism, and Neurath's boat.
notes.back: Foundationalism: justification rests on basic beliefs that need no further support. Coherentism: beliefs are justified by mutual support in a web. Neurath: we are sailors rebuilding our ship at sea, plank by plank — no dry dock of certain foundations, but not everything can be doubted at once.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Reliabilism (Goldman).
notes.back: A belief is justified iff produced by a reliable process (one with a high truth ratio), whether or not the believer can articulate reasons. Externalist: justification is about the process, not the believer's introspective access. Underpins trusting instruments and track records.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Scientific realism: the 'no miracles' argument versus the pessimistic meta-induction.
notes.back:
No miracles (Putnam): the success of mature science would be a miracle unless its theories were approximately true.
Pessimistic meta-induction (Laudan 1981): most past successful theories (phlogiston, caloric, ether) turned out false, so current ones probably will too.
Middle positions: structural realism (retain the maths, not the ontology).

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Van Fraassen's constructive empiricism.
notes.back: Science aims at empirical adequacy (getting the observables right), not truth about unobservables. Acceptance of a theory involves belief only that it is empirically adequate. A principled way to use theories heavily while withholding ontological commitment.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Theory-ladenness of observation.
notes.back: There is no neutral observation language: what counts as data depends on the concepts and instruments brought to it (Hanson: Tycho and Kepler 'see' different sunrises). Does not make observation worthless; it means observation reports carry assumptions that can themselves be tested.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Whewell's consilience of inductions.
notes.back: A theory gains strong support when it explains classes of facts it was not built to explain — different kinds of evidence 'jump together'. Newton's gravity covering tides, planets, and falling bodies. Novel-prediction success and consilience are the main non-Bayesian intuitions Bayesians try to recover.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Bradford Hill's viewpoints for inferring causation from observational data (1965).
notes.back:
Strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient (dose–response), plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy.
Hill explicitly said none is necessary or sufficient (except temporality) and rejected treating them as a checklist. Still the standard vocabulary for causal argument without a randomised trial.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Pearl's ladder of causation.
notes.back: Rung 1 Association: seeing, P(y|x). Rung 2 Intervention: doing, P(y|do(x)). Rung 3 Counterfactuals: imagining, P(y_x | x', y'). Observational data alone lives on rung 1; causal claims need rung 2 assumptions (a causal graph) or actual intervention. Correlation is not causation, formalised.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Why a Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) is privileged, and its two main limits.
notes.back: Randomisation makes treatment independent of all confounders, known and unknown, so the difference in outcomes identifies the causal effect. Limits: external validity (result may not transfer to other populations/settings) and it estimates an average effect, which can hide heterogeneous or opposite individual effects.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: The replication crisis: Ioannidis's argument and the structural fixes.
notes.back: Ioannidis (2005): with low prior probability of hypotheses, low power, flexible analysis, and publication bias, most published positive findings are false. Fixes: preregistration, registered reports, larger samples, sharing data and code, multi-lab replication. Reproducibility Project (2015): ~36% of psychology findings replicated.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Base-rate neglect, with the medical-test illustration.
notes.back: Test 99% sensitive and 99% specific; disease prevalence 1 in 10,000. A positive result implies P(disease) ≈ 1%, not 99%, because false positives (~100 per million) swamp true positives (~99 per million). Likelihood ratios must be combined with priors; the prior is usually the dominant term for rare events.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: The reference class problem.
notes.back: The probability you assign depends on which class you put the case in (a 40-year-old smoker: all 40-year-olds? all smokers? all 40-year-old smokers?). No unique correct class; narrower classes are more relevant but have less data. Every base rate embeds a choice.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Occam's razor: its three justifications and their status.
notes.back: (1) Pragmatic: simpler theories are easier to test and use. (2) Bayesian/statistical: complex models fit noise (overfitting); simpler models generalise better — Minimum Description Length and Solomonoff induction formalise this. (3) Metaphysical: nature is simple — unsupported. Only (1) and (2) carry weight.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Calibration, and what Tetlock found about good forecasters.
notes.back: A forecaster is calibrated if events they assign 70% happen ~70% of the time; scored by Brier score. Tetlock: experts barely beat chance; foxes (many small models, updating) beat hedgehogs (one big idea). Superforecasters update in small increments, decompose questions, and use base rates first.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: 'Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' — when is this false?
notes.back: It is false whenever you would expect to see evidence if the hypothesis were true. If P(E | H) is high and you do not observe E, that is evidence against H by the likelihood ratio. The slogan only holds when the search would not have found E anyway.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Sagan's 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' in Bayesian terms.
notes.back: A claim with low prior odds needs a large likelihood ratio to reach a credible posterior. Not a special rule: it is Bayes' theorem applied to low priors. Corollary: the more surprising the claim, the more you should suspect error, fraud, or misinterpretation in the evidence itself.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Simpson's paradox.
notes.back: A trend present in every subgroup reverses when the groups are pooled, because of an unequal distribution of a confounder across groups (Berkeley admissions 1973). Whether to trust the pooled or stratified result depends on the causal structure, not the numbers — which is why it needs a causal graph.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Berkson's paradox (collider bias).
notes.back: Conditioning on a common effect of two independent causes induces a spurious correlation between them. Hospital patients: two independent diseases appear negatively correlated because having either gets you admitted. Selection effects are causal errors, not just sampling errors.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Goodhart's law and its relevance to evidence.
notes.back: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Any proxy under optimisation pressure decouples from the thing it proxied (citations, test scores, KPIs). An epistemic warning: evidence generated by parties who benefit from it needs a discount factor.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Meehl's clinical vs statistical prediction.
notes.back: Across ~20 studies (1954) and ~136 later (Grove et al. 2000), simple actuarial formulas matched or beat expert clinical judgement in almost every domain. Humans add noise; experts are best at choosing variables, worst at combining them. Argument for structured, mechanical aggregation of evidence.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Regression to the mean as an epistemic trap.
notes.back: Extreme measurements are partly luck; the next measurement will tend toward the mean regardless of any intervention. Interventions applied after bad outcomes (punishment, crisis programmes) look effective; ones applied after good outcomes look harmful. Requires a control group to distinguish.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Feynman's 'cargo cult science' and the principle of 'leaning over backwards'.
notes.back: Scientific integrity means reporting everything that could invalidate your result, not just what supports it — "the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool." Cargo-cult science copies the form of science (papers, methods) without this norm.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Peirce's fallibilism.
notes.back: Any belief may turn out false, yet this is no reason for doubt without a specific ground: "Do not block the way of inquiry." Beliefs are provisional but action-guiding; genuine doubt arises from surprise, not from Cartesian resolution. The pragmatist template for provisional commitment.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Chesterton's fence.
notes.back: Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put there. Existing practices encode information (often about failures) that is not visible in the practice itself. A conservatism heuristic that is really about hidden evidence, not tradition.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Aumann's agreement theorem and what it implies about persistent disagreement.
notes.back: Two Bayesians with common priors and common knowledge of each other's posteriors cannot agree to disagree — their posteriors must be equal. Since real people do persist, at least one of: different priors, private information not shared, or one party is not updating rationally. Persistent disagreement is diagnostic.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Value of information (VoI): the decision-theoretic test for whether evidence is worth collecting.
notes.back: Information has value only if it could change a decision. Expected value of perfect information = expected value with the information minus expected value of the best action without it. Evidence that would leave you doing the same thing is worthless for that decision, however interesting.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Immunising stratagems (Popper) and how to recognise a degenerating position.
notes.back: Moves that protect a theory from refutation: ad hoc auxiliary hypotheses, redefining terms, questioning the observer's motives, shifting to unfalsifiable formulations. Test: ask the proponent in advance what observation would count against the view. A position with no answer has become unfalsifiable in practice.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::2 Philosophy of Science and Epistemology
notes.front: Epistemic vs instrumental rationality.
notes.back: Epistemic: forming beliefs that track truth (updating on evidence). Instrumental: choosing actions that achieve goals. They can conflict — a false belief may be useful. Keeping them separate lets you notice when you are motivated to believe something because it would be convenient.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Consequentialism vs deontology vs virtue ethics: the locus of moral evaluation in each.
notes.back: Consequentialism: outcomes (utilitarianism = maximise aggregate welfare). Deontology: the act itself — duties, rights, constraints that hold regardless of outcome. Virtue ethics: the agent's character and practical wisdom (phronesis). Most applied disputes are about which locus dominates when they conflict.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Act vs rule utilitarianism, and why rule utilitarianism keeps collapsing.
notes.back: Act: do whatever maximises utility in this case. Rule: follow rules whose general adoption maximises utility. Objection: if a rule has an exception that increases utility, the rule utilitarian must add it, and iterating this collapses into act utilitarianism. Defence: rules have coordination and error-correction value that case-by-case judgement lacks.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Kant's categorical imperative: the two main formulations.
notes.back: Universal law: act only on maxims you could will to be universal laws (lying fails: universal lying destroys the trust that lying exploits). Humanity: treat persons always as ends in themselves, never merely as means. The second grounds consent and dignity requirements in modern ethics and law.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean and phronesis.
notes.back: Virtue is a disposition to feel and act at the right amount, at the right time, toward the right people — between excess and deficiency (courage between rashness and cowardice). Finding it requires phronesis (practical wisdom), which cannot be reduced to rules. Argument against fully codifiable ethics.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Rawls: original position, veil of ignorance, and the two principles of justice.
notes.back: Choose principles not knowing your position, talents, or conception of the good. Result: (1) equal basic liberties for all; (2) inequalities permitted only if (a) attached to positions open under fair equality of opportunity and (b) they benefit the least advantaged (difference principle). Lexical priority: 1 over 2, 2a over 2b.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Rawls's public reason and overlapping consensus.
notes.back: In a pluralist society, coercive political decisions must be justifiable in terms citizens with different comprehensive doctrines could accept — public reason. Stability comes from an overlapping consensus: each doctrine endorses the political conception for its own reasons. Template for legitimate rules under deep disagreement.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Nozick's entitlement theory and the Wilt Chamberlain argument.
notes.back: Justice in holdings = just acquisition + just transfer + rectification; no patterned end-state. Chamberlain: start from any just distribution, let fans voluntarily pay to watch him play; the result is unequal but every step was just — so liberty upsets patterns, and maintaining a pattern requires continuous interference.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Scanlon's contractualism.
notes.back: An act is wrong if it would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behaviour that no one could reasonably reject. Justification is owed to each person individually, not to the aggregate — hence it blocks sacrificing one for many where utilitarianism would not.
notes.source: Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (1998)

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: The trolley problem and the doctrine of double effect.
notes.back: Switch (kill 1 to save 5): most say yes. Footbridge (push 1 to save 5): most say no. Double effect: harm that is a foreseen side-effect of a good act may be permissible; harm used as a means is not. Whether this distinction is morally real is the live question — and it is exactly what an automated system's objective must encode or ignore.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Parfit's repugnant conclusion.
notes.back: For any large population with very high welfare, there is a much larger population with lives barely worth living that total utilitarianism ranks as better. Every population axiology violates some intuitively compelling condition (Arrhenius impossibility theorems). Aggregate-welfare objectives have unresolved foundations at scale.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Moral uncertainty: the problem and the main proposals.
notes.back: You are uncertain not only about facts but about which moral theory is correct. Proposals: 'my favourite theory' (act on the most probable one), maximise expected choiceworthiness (weight options by credence in each theory — needs intertheoretic comparability), or a moral parliament (bargaining among theories). No consensus; the question matters for anyone specifying objectives for others.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Hume's is–ought gap and Moore's naturalistic fallacy.
notes.back: Hume: no valid inference from purely descriptive premises to a normative conclusion. Moore: identifying 'good' with any natural property (pleasure, evolutionary fitness) is a fallacy, exposed by the open question argument ('X is pleasant, but is it good?' remains meaningful). Implication: data cannot settle values; a value premise must be supplied explicitly.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Hobbes: the state of nature and why a sovereign is rational.
notes.back: Without a common power life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a war of all against all driven by competition, diffidence, and glory. Rational individuals contract to transfer their rights to a sovereign that enforces peace. First systematic argument that enforceable authority is a precondition for cooperation.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Locke: natural rights, consent, and the labour theory of property.
notes.back: Life, liberty, and property are pre-political rights; government is legitimate only by consent and only to protect them; a government that violates them may be resisted. Property arises by mixing labour with unowned nature, subject to the proviso that 'enough and as good' is left for others.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Rousseau's general will.
notes.back: Legitimacy comes from the general will: the will directed at the common good, distinct from the will of all (sum of private interests). Citizens obey laws they gave themselves and so remain free. Worry: who decides what the general will is — the opening for 'forcing people to be free'.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Mill's harm principle.
notes.back: The only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over a member of a civilised community against their will is to prevent harm to others; their own good is not sufficient warrant. Anti-paternalism baseline; the hard part is what counts as 'harm' (offence? risk? indirect harm?).

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Berlin: negative vs positive liberty.
notes.back: Negative: absence of interference by others. Positive: self-mastery, being one's own master, having the capacity to act. Berlin warned that positive liberty can be twisted into coercion in the name of the 'true self'. Design question: is a system that removes options to protect you increasing or decreasing freedom?

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Pettit's republican liberty as non-domination.
notes.back: Freedom is not merely non-interference but the absence of arbitrary power over you — a kind master's slave is unfree even if never interfered with. Requires that power be constrained, contestable, and accountable. Directly applicable to platforms and automated systems that could act against users at will.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Weber's three types of legitimate authority.
notes.back: Traditional (it has always been so), charismatic (the leader's extraordinary qualities), legal-rational (rules enacted by proper procedure, administered impersonally by a bureaucracy). Modern states run on the third; automated decision systems inherit its demand for procedural regularity.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Fuller's inner morality of law: the eight desiderata.
notes.back: Laws must be (1) general, (2) promulgated, (3) prospective not retroactive, (4) clear, (5) non-contradictory, (6) possible to comply with, (7) stable over time, (8) congruent with how they are actually administered. A system failing these is not merely bad law but not law. Useful checklist for any rule-enforcing system, including automated ones.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Montesquieu and the separation of powers.
notes.back: Liberty requires that legislative, executive, and judicial powers be in different hands, so that each checks the others. Principle behind constitutional design and, by analogy, the argument against one actor building, deploying, and auditing the same system.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Habermas's discourse ethics and the ideal speech situation.
notes.back: A norm is valid only if all affected could accept it in a rational discourse free of coercion, where only the force of the better argument counts. Legitimacy is procedural: it comes from the quality of the deliberation, not the content of the outcome. Basis of deliberative democracy theory.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Arrow's impossibility theorem.
notes.back: No ranked voting rule with three or more options can satisfy all of: unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship. Every aggregation of preferences is a trade-off; there is no neutral way to combine individual rankings into a social one. Applies to aggregating stakeholder values in any system.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Condorcet's jury theorem and its assumptions.
notes.back: If each voter is independently more likely than not to be correct on a binary question, the majority's probability of being correct rises toward 1 with group size. Fails if competence is below ½ (majority converges to wrong) or if votes are correlated (shared information, herding). Justifies aggregation only under independence.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Hardin's tragedy of the commons vs Ostrom's findings.
notes.back: Hardin (1968): open-access resources are inevitably overused; only privatisation or state control can save them. Ostrom: communities worldwide sustainably self-govern commons without either, given the right institutional design. Hardin described open access, not commons; commons have rules.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Ostrom's eight design principles for durable commons institutions.
notes.back: (1) Clear boundaries, (2) rules fitted to local conditions, (3) those affected can modify rules, (4) monitoring by accountable monitors, (5) graduated sanctions, (6) cheap conflict-resolution mechanisms, (7) minimal recognition of the right to organise by higher authorities, (8) nested enterprises for larger systems. Empirically derived; a governance checklist.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Subsidiarity.
notes.back: Decisions should be taken at the lowest level competent to take them; higher levels intervene only where lower ones cannot achieve the objective. Origin in Catholic social teaching; codified in EU treaties. A principle for allocating governance authority across layers of a system.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Externalities and the Pigouvian argument for regulation.
notes.back: When an actor's costs fall on third parties (pollution, systemic risk), private optimisation overproduces the harm. Pigou: tax the activity at the marginal external cost. Coase: with low transaction costs, bargaining fixes it regardless of initial rights — so regulation is justified precisely where bargaining is infeasible (many victims, diffuse harm).

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Principal–agent problem and moral hazard.
notes.back: An agent acting for a principal has private information and divergent interests; the principal cannot fully observe effort. Moral hazard: insulated from consequences, the agent takes more risk. Solutions: monitoring, incentive alignment, bonding, liability. Core frame for delegation to any autonomous system.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Precommitment: Ulysses and constitutional constraints.
notes.back: Ulysses binds himself to the mast so his later self cannot act on the Sirens' call. Constitutions are collective precommitment: a supermajority past restrains a simple-majority present against predictable temptations. Elster: rational agents sometimes increase welfare by removing their own future options.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Popper's paradox of tolerance and piecemeal social engineering.
notes.back: Unlimited tolerance leads to the disappearance of tolerance: a tolerant society must reserve the right to suppress the intolerant when argument fails. Popper also rejected utopian blueprints for piecemeal engineering — small, reversible reforms whose effects can be tested. Governance as falsifiable experiment.
notes.source: Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945)

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Precautionary principle vs proactionary principle.
notes.back: Precautionary: where an activity threatens serious or irreversible harm, lack of full scientific certainty is not a reason to postpone preventive measures (burden on the proponent). Proactionary (More): the costs of forgone innovation count too; burden on those who would restrict. Neither resolves the Collingridge dilemma; they allocate the burden of proof differently.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Lessig: 'code is law' and the four modalities of regulation.
notes.back: Behaviour is regulated by law, norms, the market, and architecture (code). Architecture regulates without needing enforcement or consent and is often invisible as regulation. Design choices in software are therefore political choices and should be evaluated as such.
notes.source: Lessig, Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace (1999)

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Nissenbaum's contextual integrity.
notes.back: Privacy is not secrecy or control but the appropriate flow of information according to the norms of the context in which it was shared (medical, financial, social). A violation is a flow that breaches context-relative norms — e.g. health data flowing to an employer — even if each party individually 'consented'.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: The impossibility of satisfying multiple fairness criteria simultaneously.
notes.back: Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017): when base rates differ between groups, a classifier cannot simultaneously be calibrated, have equal false-positive rates, and equal false-negative rates (except in trivial cases). Choosing a fairness metric is a substantive ethical decision, not a technical one — COMPAS debate.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: The responsibility gap and the problem of many hands.
notes.back: Many hands (Thompson 1980): in large organisations outcomes result from so many contributions that no individual is responsible. Responsibility gap (Matthias 2004): with learning systems, neither the manufacturer nor the operator can foresee behaviour well enough to be fairly held responsible. Both argue for designing accountability structures in advance rather than assigning blame after.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Moral luck.
notes.back: Two equally reckless drivers; one hits a child. We judge them differently though the only difference is luck. Nagel: resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal luck all infect moral assessment, yet we cannot abandon it. Implication for design: outcome-based blame is systematically unfair; evaluate decisions by the information available at the time.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Kant's 'ought implies can'.
notes.back: A moral obligation presupposes the ability to fulfil it; one cannot be required to do the impossible. Corollary for governance: rules imposed on agents (or systems) that cannot comply are not obligations but traps — cf. Fuller's desideratum (6).

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach.
notes.back: Evaluate justice not by resources or welfare but by what people are actually able to do and be (capabilities), given their circumstances — the same income yields different real freedom for a disabled and an able-bodied person. Nussbaum lists central capabilities as a threshold every society must guarantee. Metric for whether a technology expands or contracts real options.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Value-sensitive design (Friedman).
notes.back: A method integrating ethical values into technical design through three iterative investigations: conceptual (which stakeholders and values, including indirect stakeholders), empirical (how they actually experience the system), technical (which design choices support or undermine the values). Values are treated as design requirements, not afterthoughts.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Meaningful human control and automation bias.
notes.back: Meaningful human control requires that humans can understand, intervene in, and be held responsible for a system's actions — not merely be present. Undermined by automation bias: people defer to automated outputs even when wrong (Parasuraman & Riley 1997). A human 'in the loop' who cannot realistically dissent provides legitimacy without control.
notes.source: Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven 2018

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Foucault: the panopticon and disciplinary power.
notes.back: Bentham's prison design lets one guard potentially observe all inmates, who, unable to know when they are watched, discipline themselves. Foucault: modern power works less by punishment than by normalising surveillance that makes subjects self-regulate. The default analytic for pervasive monitoring systems.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Arendt: the banality of evil.
notes.back: Eichmann was not a monster but a thoughtless functionary who followed procedure and clichés without judging. Great harm can be produced by ordinary people in bureaucratic roles who have outsourced judgement to the system. Warning about process compliance as a substitute for moral thinking.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Procedural vs substantive justice, and the right to reasons.
notes.back: Procedural: fair process (notice, hearing, impartial decider, reasons, appeal). Substantive: correct outcome. Administrative law generally requires reasons for adverse decisions because reasons enable contestation and check arbitrariness; the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 22 extends a version of this to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Ross's prima facie duties.
notes.back: Fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence. Each is binding prima facie; when they conflict, no fixed ranking decides — judgement does. A pluralist alternative to single-principle theories, and a realistic model of how practitioners actually reason.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::3 Ethics and Political Philosophy
notes.front: Care ethics.
notes.back: Morality centres on relationships, responsiveness to particular others, and attentiveness to dependency — not impartial principles applied to abstract agents. Criticises the assumption of independent, equal contractors in liberal theory. Relevant where a system mediates relationships of dependence (health, care, education).
notes.source: Gilligan, In a Different Voice (1982); Noddings; Held
